analysis.one_liner: Delays Clean Air Act carbon limits on power plants until every lawsuit finishes and lets governors opt out.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 247-180 in June 2015, but the Senate placed it on a calendar and never voted, and it died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill was aimed at the EPA's rules limiting carbon dioxide emissions from existing coal- and gas-fired power plants. It would have pushed every compliance deadline back until all court challenges to the rule were fully finished, which could take years. It would also have let any state governor declare, after notifying EPA, that the plan would hurt the state's electricity ratepayers or grid reliability — and then block both the state plan and any federal plan imposed in its place. It also directed EPA to treat hydropower as renewable energy in carrying out the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal-fired and other fossil-fuel power plants, and coal-producing states, gain the most: the bill delays emission limits for as long as any lawsuit is pending and gives governors a unilateral exit that could prevent the rules from applying at all. Some households and businesses in states with high compliance costs could avoid rate increases, which is the benefit the bill's sponsors emphasized.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal-fired power plant owners and coal states

how_it_helps.text: Every compliance date for EPA carbon rules on existing fossil-fuel power plants — including state plan submission deadlines — is pushed back until litigation filed within 60 days of a final rule is fully resolved, with no further appeal [S3][S5].

A governor can unilaterally block both the state implementation plan and any substitute federal plan by notifying EPA that the plan would significantly harm the state's ratepayers or grid reliability [S3][S5].
EPA must treat hydropower as renewable energy when implementing or enforcing the rules, and the bill urges EPA to credit pumped hydro storage in state and federal plans [S4][S5].

analysis.who_pays: The costs of delayed carbon limits fall on people exposed to power plant pollution and on future generations bearing climate damages; cleaner energy industries lose near-term demand the rules would have created. Households still pay the climate and health costs of continued emissions even where short-term electricity bills are spared.
analysis.who_pays_short: Residents exposed to plant pollution; clean energy industries

drawbacks.text: The governor opt-out has no objective standard for what counts as a 'significant adverse effect,' so any governor could block a state plan or a federal fallback, effectively making compliance with the carbon rules voluntary [S5].
Because the delay runs until judicial review is completely finished and unappealable, litigation could postpone the rules for years, during which power plants would face no carbon limits [S3][S5].
Supporters of the underlying EPA rule argue that delaying emissions limits shifts costs onto the public as health and climate damages, rather than eliminating them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Concern about electricity prices and grid reliability is genuine, and the bill did require governors to consult state utility and environmental agencies before opting out. But the opt-out has no measurable threshold, and combined with a compliance delay that lasts through the entire life of any lawsuit, the bill's practical effect would be to suspend or void the carbon rules rather than fine-tune consumer protection. The ratepayer framing is a modest protection wrapped around a much larger delay of the underlying regulation.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill 247-180 on June 24, 2015, but the Senate only received it and placed it on its calendar — it never came up for a vote — and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The House Committee on Energy and Commerce ordered the bill reported by a 28-22 vote and reported it on June 19, 2015 [S7].
On June 24, 2015, the House passed the bill 247-180, with 239 of 245 Republicans voting yes and only 8 of 188 Democrats [S7][S8].
The Senate received the bill on June 25, 2015; it sat until July 14, 2016, when it was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, and no vote was ever held [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, power plant operators did not get a litigation-length delay or a governor-level escape hatch from the EPA's carbon rules, which remained in effect while the courts reviewed them. The outcome was shaped mostly by the House's near party-line passage and the Senate's failure to act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA's power plant carbon rules stood; operators got no delay

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: His administration opposed the bill as an attempt to delay the Clean Power Plan; it died without reaching his desk.

sides.party_line_note: The final vote split almost perfectly by party: 239 of 245 Republicans voted yes and only 8 of 188 Democrats did, for a 247-180 total.

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired electric utilities
industries.note: The bill's core provisions would have delayed or excused them from carbon emission limits on existing power plants, potentially for the entire life of any lawsuit or indefinitely via a governor's opt-out. Their gain comes from avoiding pollution controls whose costs the public bears as health and climate damages.

Delaying the Clean Power Plan compliance dates spares utilities near-term compliance spending on generation and infrastructure changes. Some of that relief could reach ratepayers, but the savings come at the cost of continued emissions.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and energy efficiency industries
industries.note: Delaying the carbon rules would have slowed the buildout of wind, solar, and efficiency investments that the rules were expected to drive. Their interest runs with the public's in cleaner air.

The bill requires EPA to count hydropower as renewable energy under the carbon rules and urges crediting pumped hydro storage, giving existing hydro operators credit toward state plans. This is a narrower provision than the bill's delay of compliance for fossil plants.
Gas plants are subject to the same delayed rules but were expected to gain market share from coal under the Clean Power Plan; delaying the rules slows that shift as well.
